title: Module 3 · Lesson 1 — Evaluating agents: what to measure and where

lines: Module Three, Lesson One: evaluating agents.
What should you measure, and where?
Picture a travel bot that books flights and hotels for an office.
One Monday, its success rate drops from eighty-two percent to seventy.
The team stares at that one number for a week.
It says something is wrong, but nothing about where.
Agent evaluation works in four layers: component, step, trajectory, and outcome.
Each one answers a different question.
Component checks test each piece alone, like retrieval recall.
Step checks grade each decision, like the tool and arguments chosen.
Trajectory checks score the whole path the agent took.
Six redundant searches and a lucky guess can pass the outcome check, yet fail on reliability.
Outcome checks ask whether the task actually got done.
Think task success, groundedness, and cost per resolved task.
For retrieval, four RAG metrics form a diagnostic grid.
Low context recall means the evidence was never fetched; high recall with low faithfulness means the model ignored it.

say.0: For retrieval, four rag metrics form a diagnostic grid.

lines: So test retrieval on its own, before the generator runs.
That exposed the travel team's culprit: hotel search was fetching the wrong listings.
A golden dataset keeps it from happening again.
It's versioned with the code, drawn from real traffic, and full of hard cases.
Source it from production traffic, synthetic data, and expert adversarial cases.
Then run it in CI on every prompt, model, or tool change.

say.1: Then run it in C I on every prompt, model, or tool change.

lines: Agents are stochastic, so one run proves nothing.
Pass@k means any of k runs succeeded; pass^k means all of them did, and production needs that.

say.1: Pass at kay means any of kay runs succeeded; pass hat kay means all of them did, and production needs that.

lines: A thirty-case suite swings about eighteen points either way.
You need hundreds of cases before small gains justify a release.
Releases then move from offline tests to shadow, canary, and full rollout.
Shadow mirrors live traffic to the new version but never serves its answers.
Exam tip: zero-risk validation on real traffic means shadow, since canary already exposes some users.
Read on for every layer in detail.
